t: Manichaeism was founded by Mani, a prophet from Sasanian Mesopotamia, who from about 240 taught that the world is a mixture of light and darkness and that souls, sparks of light, can be freed through knowledge and discipline.

Organised into an elite of the Elect and a laity of Hearers, it spread west into the Roman Empire, where the young Augustine of Hippo was a Hearer, and east along the Silk Road to the Uyghurs and China.
Persecuted by Zoroastrian, Christian, Muslim and Chinese rulers alike, it disappeared by the early modern period, leaving its name to any world view that divides everything into good and evil.
dyk: A temple at Cao’an near Quanzhou in southern China still holds a stone image of Mani as the “Buddha of Light”, carved in 1339: the only Manichaean shrine in the world known to survive.
ev: Mani is born in Mesopotamia, near the Persian capital Ctesiphon
Mani begins to preach his religion, after a revelation in his youth
Mani dies in prison under the Sasanian king Bahram I
The Roman emperor Diocletian orders the persecution of the Manichaeans
Augustine of Hippo is a Manichaean Hearer before his conversion to Christianity
The Uyghur ruler Bögü Qaghan adopts Manichaeism, the faith of his empire for decades
The Tang emperor Wuzong bans Manichaeism in China
The image of Mani as the Buddha of Light is carved at Cao’an near Quanzhou

f.founder: The prophet Mani (216–about 276), who claimed to complete the teachings of Zoroaster, the Buddha and Jesus
f.scriptures: The seven books of Mani, his Shabuhragan and his Picture Book, known today mainly from fragments found in Egypt and Central Asia
f.followers: None today: the last communities, in southern China, faded after the 16th century
